question: A 78-year-old woman attends for a routine ECG. She is asymptomatic. The ECG shows: regular P waves at 72/min, followed by progressively lengthening PR intervals over 3 beats, then a dropped QRS, then the cycle repeats. Per NICE and ESC guidelines, what is this ECG pattern and management?

options.A: Complete heart block — permanent pacemaker immediately
options.B: Mobitz Type I (Wenckebach) second-degree AV block — progressive PR prolongation then a dropped beat; in asymptomatic patients, particularly when associated with inferior MI or vagal tone, this is often benign; monitor, avoid AV-nodal blocking drugs (beta-blockers, digoxin, verapamil, diltiazem), refer to cardiology for assessment
options.C: First-degree heart block — no action required
options.D: Mobitz Type II second-degree AV block — requires urgent pacing
options.E: Atrial flutter with variable block — rate control with digoxin

explanation.correct: Mobitz Type I (Wenckebach) second-degree AV block: progressive PR interval lengthening over consecutive beats until one P wave fails to conduct (dropped QRS), then the cycle resets. Distinguished from Mobitz II (sudden dropped beat without PR prolongation). Wenckebach characteristics: block is typically at the level of the AV node (proximal); associated with: inferior MI (RCA supplies AV node), vagal tone, myocarditis, beta-blocker/calcium channel blocker/digoxin toxicity. Prognosis: generally benign in the absence of structural heart disease or symptoms. Management per ESC Pacing Guidelines: asymptomatic Wenckebach — no pacing required; avoid AV-nodal blocking drugs; cardiology review; treat reversible causes. If symptomatic (dizziness, syncope, pre-syncope) — pacemaker may be indicated. Mobitz II (sudden dropped beats, often wide QRS escape) carries higher risk of progression to complete heart block and is more often a pacing indication.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Complete heart block has AV dissociation (P and QRS completely independent). Wenckebach has a maintained relationship with progressive PR lengthening before the dropped beat.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Mobitz I (Wenckebach): progressive PR prolongation then dropped beat. Benign in asymptomatic patient; avoid AV-nodal drugs; cardiology review per ESC guidelines.
explanation.C: Incorrect — First-degree AV block has a prolonged but constant PR interval with every P wave conducting. There are no dropped beats.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Mobitz Type II shows sudden dropped beats (no preceding PR prolongation) and is a higher-risk finding that more often requires pacing. This is Wenckebach (Type I).
explanation.E: Incorrect — Atrial flutter shows a characteristic sawtooth atrial pattern at ~300/min with variable ventricular response. This ECG has sinus P waves.

reference: ESC Guidelines on Cardiac Pacing 2021. https://www.escardio.org/Guidelines

question: A 65-year-old man presents with two episodes of syncope. His ECG shows: regular P waves with a constant PR interval, then sudden dropped QRS complexes (2:1 pattern — every other P wave blocked). The QRS when present is wide (0.16 seconds) with LBBB morphology. Per ESC guidelines, what is the risk of this ECG and management?

options.A: Mobitz I (Wenckebach) — benign; reassure and discharge
options.B: Mobitz Type II second-degree AV block with LBBB — high risk of progression to complete heart block and sudden cardiac death; the wide QRS indicates block below the AV node (infranodal — His-Purkinje system); syncope with this pattern is an indication for urgent permanent pacemaker implantation; admit same-day for cardiology assessment
options.C: First-degree AV block — no treatment required
options.D: Ventricular tachycardia — synchronised DC cardioversion
options.E: Physiological AV block from athletic training — no treatment

explanation.correct: Mobitz Type II second-degree AV block: sudden dropped beats WITHOUT preceding PR prolongation; PR interval is constant when beats do conduct. The wide QRS (LBBB morphology) indicates the block is at the infranodal level (His-Purkinje system) — below the AV node. This is a high-risk finding: infranodal block can deteriorate without warning into complete heart block and asystole. Risk factors indicating urgent pacing: Mobitz II + wide QRS complex (infranodal) + syncope. Per ESC Cardiac Pacing Guidelines 2021: Mobitz II with symptoms (syncope/pre-syncope) is a Class I indication for permanent pacemaker, particularly when the QRS is wide. Even asymptomatic Mobitz II with wide QRS is often a pacing indication (Class IIa). Same-day hospital admission and cardiology assessment is essential.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Wenckebach (Mobitz I) has progressive PR prolongation before the dropped beat. This ECG shows sudden dropped beats with constant PR (Mobitz II). These are different diagnoses with very different prognoses.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Mobitz II + LBBB + syncope: high risk of progression to complete heart block. Urgent permanent pacemaker per ESC 2021 (Class I indication).
explanation.C: Incorrect — First-degree block has prolonged but constant PR with all P waves conducting. This has dropped beats.
explanation.D: Incorrect — This is a conduction block, not a tachyarrhythmia. Cardioversion is inappropriate.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Athletic AV block is vagally mediated Wenckebach during sleep/rest — not Mobitz II with wide QRS in a symptomatic older adult.

reference: ESC Guidelines on Cardiac Pacing 2021. https://www.escardio.org/Guidelines

question: A 62-year-old man presents with an anterior STEMI and is taken for primary PCI. Post-procedure, his ECG shows new ST elevation in leads V1-V4 persisting at 48 hours along with a new pansystolic murmur. Per cardiology guidelines, what complication should be suspected?

options.A: Pericarditis — common after MI, treat with aspirin and colchicine
options.B: Ventricular septal defect (VSD) — a mechanical complication of anterior MI (LAD territory) typically occurring 3-7 days post-STEMI; septal necrosis causes an acute left-to-right shunt; presents with new pansystolic murmur, haemodynamic deterioration and oxygenation step-up from right atrium to pulmonary artery; requires urgent echocardiogram; high mortality without surgical/percutaneous closure
options.C: Acute mitral regurgitation from papillary muscle rupture — inferior MI more commonly causes this
options.D: Right ventricular infarction — treated with IV fluids and avoiding nitrates
options.E: Dressler syndrome — autoimmune pericarditis 2-10 weeks post-MI

explanation.correct: Post-STEMI mechanical complications — rare but life-threatening: (1) Ventricular septal defect (VSD): occurs 3-7 days post-anterior MI (LAD/septal branches); septal wall necrosis → rupture → left-to-right shunt; presentation: new loud pansystolic murmur (louder at left sternal edge), acute haemodynamic deterioration, pulmonary oedema, cardiogenic shock. Diagnosis: bedside echo (step-up in O2 saturation from RA to PA on right heart catheter). Treatment: urgent surgical repair or percutaneous closure; high mortality. (2) Papillary muscle rupture → acute mitral regurgitation: occurs with inferior MI (posterior papillary muscle — RCA territory); softer murmur radiating to axilla; pulmonary oedema. (3) Free wall rupture → haemopericardium, tamponade, death. The pansystolic murmur at 48 hours post-anterior STEMI = VSD until proven otherwise.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Post-MI pericarditis (early) causes pleuritic chest pain and a friction rub — not a new pansystolic murmur with haemodynamic change.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Post-anterior STEMI pansystolic murmur = VSD until proven otherwise. Urgent echo + cardiology/cardiac surgery per guidelines.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Papillary muscle rupture causes acute MR and is more common after inferior MI (posterior papillary muscle from RCA). Anterior STEMI more commonly causes VSD.
explanation.D: Incorrect — RV infarction (inferior/posterior MI) causes elevated JVP, hypotension, clear lungs. Not associated with anterior STEMI + new murmur.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Dressler syndrome occurs 2-10 weeks post-MI and causes pleuritic chest pain with pericardial effusion — not an acute pansystolic murmur at 48 hours.

reference: ESC Guidelines — Management of STEMI. https://www.escardio.org/Guidelines

question: A GP is reviewing the ECG of a 55-year-old man and notices: no P waves, an irregular baseline with fine fibrillatory waves at 350-600/min, and an irregular ventricular response at 90/min with narrow QRS complexes. Per NICE NG196, what is this rhythm and initial management?

options.A: Atrial flutter — refer for DC cardioversion
options.B: Atrial fibrillation (AF) — most common sustained cardiac arrhythmia; requires assessment of: stroke risk (CHA₂DS₂-VASc score for anticoagulation decision), ventricular rate control (target <110 bpm at rest using beta-blocker or calcium channel blocker), and consideration of rhythm control (cardioversion, antiarrhythmic drugs, ablation); exclude reversible causes (thyroid disease, infection)
options.C: Sinus tachycardia — reassure and monitor
options.D: Ventricular fibrillation — emergency defibrillation immediately
options.E: Junctional rhythm — no treatment required

explanation.correct: Atrial fibrillation (AF): no organised P waves (replaced by fine fibrillatory baseline), irregularly irregular ventricular response, narrow QRS (unless aberrant conduction). Affects approximately 1.5 million in the UK — most common sustained arrhythmia. Per NICE NG196: (1) Rate control: first-line in most patients; target resting HR <110 bpm; use beta-blocker (bisoprolol) or rate-limiting CCB (diltiazem, verapamil); digoxin for sedentary patients or as add-on. (2) Stroke prevention: CHA₂DS₂-VASc score ≥1 (men), ≥2 (women) = anticoagulate with DOAC (apixaban, rivaroxaban, edoxaban, dabigatran) or warfarin; assess bleeding risk (ORBIT score). (3) Rhythm control: for symptomatic AF despite rate control, younger patients, recent onset; options: cardioversion, antiarrhythmics (flecainide if no structural disease; amiodarone), AF ablation. (4) Investigate and treat reversible causes: TFTs, FBC, renal function, echocardiogram.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Atrial flutter has a regular sawtooth atrial pattern at ~300/min and usually a regular ventricular rate (150/min in 2:1 block). This ECG is irregularly irregular with fibrillatory baseline — AF.
explanation.B: CORRECT — AF: irregularly irregular, no P waves. NICE NG196: rate control + CHA₂DS₂-VASc-guided anticoagulation + consider rhythm control.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Sinus tachycardia has regular P waves before each QRS with a rate 100-150/min. This has no P waves and is irregular.
explanation.D: Incorrect — VF shows chaotic high-amplitude disorganised activity with no discernible QRS complexes — a cardiac arrest rhythm. This patient has a pulse with organised QRS complexes.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Junctional rhythm has narrow QRS with absent or inverted P waves near the QRS at a rate of 40-60/min. Not the irregular AF pattern described.

reference: NICE NG196 — Atrial fibrillation. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng196

question: A 32-year-old man presents with a 6-month history of inflammatory low back pain (worse at night, better with exercise, morning stiffness >45 minutes), bilateral buttock pain and anterior uveitis. His CRP is 28 mg/L. Per NICE NG65, what is the most likely diagnosis and key investigation?

options.A: Lumbar disc prolapse — MRI lumbar spine urgently
options.B: Axial spondyloarthritis (axSpA) / ankylosing spondylitis — characterised by inflammatory back pain, sacroiliitis, HLA-B27 positivity (90% of AS); uveitis is a classic extra-articular feature; HLA-B27 blood test and MRI sacroiliac joints (detects early sacroiliitis before X-ray changes); refer to rheumatology
options.C: Reactive arthritis — check for preceding STI or GI infection
options.D: Fibromyalgia — amitriptyline and pain management programme
options.E: Osteoporotic vertebral fractures — DEXA scan

explanation.correct: Axial spondyloarthritis (axSpA) including ankylosing spondylitis: a seronegative spondyloarthropathy characterised by inflammatory back pain and sacroiliitis. Inflammatory back pain features (per ASAS criteria): onset <40 years, insidious onset, improvement with exercise (not rest), worse at night/morning, responds to NSAIDs. Extra-articular manifestations: anterior uveitis (25-40% — recurrent acute unilateral iritis), psoriasis, inflammatory bowel disease, aortic regurgitation. Per NICE NG65 (Spondyloarthritis): HLA-B27 testing (positive in ~90% of ankylosing spondylitis in white Europeans); MRI sacroiliac joints (detects bone marrow oedema/sacroiliitis before X-ray erosions appear — crucial for early diagnosis); refer to rheumatology. Treatment: regular NSAIDs (first-line); physiotherapy; anti-TNF biologics if inadequate response to 2 NSAIDs (adalimumab, etanercept); IL-17 inhibitors (secukinumab).
explanation.A: Incorrect — Mechanical back pain (disc prolapse) is worse with activity, better at rest, and does not cause morning stiffness >45 minutes or uveitis.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Axial spondyloarthritis: inflammatory back pain + uveitis + raised CRP. HLA-B27 + MRI SIJ per NICE NG65.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Reactive arthritis (formerly Reiter's) presents within weeks of a triggering infection with asymmetric peripheral arthritis and urethritis — not a 6-month history of back pain with uveitis.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Fibromyalgia causes widespread musculoskeletal pain with normal inflammatory markers — CRP 28 mg/L and uveitis argue strongly against fibromyalgia.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Osteoporotic fractures occur in elderly patients with mechanical pain — not a young man with inflammatory back pain, raised CRP and uveitis.

reference: NICE NG65 — Spondyloarthritis. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng65

question: A 28-year-old man with confirmed ankylosing spondylitis has failed 2 NSAIDs. His BASDAI score is 5.2 (range 0-10). Per NICE TA383 and TA28, what is the next treatment option?

options.A: Oral methotrexate — first DMARD in axial spondyloarthritis
options.B: Anti-TNF biologic therapy (e.g. adalimumab, etanercept, infliximab, certolizumab) — indicated when BASDAI ≥4 after failure of 2 or more NSAIDs; approved by NICE TA383; alternatively IL-17A inhibitor (secukinumab or ixekizumab — NICE TA407) is equally effective and first-line biologic option; exclude TB and hepatitis B before starting
options.C: Oral prednisolone long-term — systemic steroids are the backbone of AS treatment
options.D: Physiotherapy alone is sufficient for BASDAI >4
options.E: Sulfasalazine — effective for axial disease in ankylosing spondylitis

explanation.correct: Per NICE TA383 (TNF-alpha inhibitors for AS) and NICE TA407 (Secukinumab for AS): biologic therapy is indicated when: BASDAI (Bath Ankylosing Spondylitis Disease Activity Index) ≥4 AND inadequate response to ≥2 NSAIDs. Anti-TNF agents: adalimumab, etanercept, infliximab, certolizumab, golimumab. IL-17 inhibitors: secukinumab, ixekizumab. Both classes are NICE-approved as first-line biologic therapy with comparable efficacy. Pre-biologic screening: TB (Mantoux/IGRA), hepatitis B/C, HIV. Important: conventional DMARDs (methotrexate, sulfasalazine) are NOT effective for axial disease in AS — they are only used for associated peripheral arthritis. Systemic corticosteroids are not a long-term treatment for AS. Physiotherapy: important adjunct throughout, but not sufficient alone for active disease (BASDAI ≥4).
explanation.A: Incorrect — Methotrexate and other conventional DMARDs are not effective for axial spondyloarthritis — they do not reduce spinal inflammation or radiographic progression.
explanation.B: CORRECT — BASDAI ≥4 after 2 NSAIDs: anti-TNF or IL-17 inhibitor per NICE TA383/TA407. Pre-screen for TB and hepatitis B.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Systemic corticosteroids are not recommended for long-term management of axial spondyloarthritis due to limited efficacy and significant side effects.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Physiotherapy is an important but insufficient treatment when BASDAI ≥4 with failed NSAIDs — biologic therapy is indicated.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Sulfasalazine has very limited evidence for axial AS; it may be considered for peripheral arthritis only — not for the spinal/sacroiliac disease.

reference: NICE TA383 — TNF-alpha inhibitors for AS. NICE TA407 — Secukinumab for AS. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ta383

question: A 48-year-old woman has palpitations occurring twice weekly, each lasting 5-10 minutes. A 7-day ambulatory ECG captures her symptoms: during palpitations the ECG shows: regular narrow complex tachycardia at 178/min with no visible P waves (or P waves buried within the QRS). Per NICE NG196, what is the most likely arrhythmia?

options.A: Atrial fibrillation — irregularly irregular narrow complex tachycardia
options.B: AV nodal re-entrant tachycardia (AVNRT) — the most common cause of regular narrow complex tachycardia (SVT) in adults; characterised by a re-entrant circuit within the AV node; P waves are absent or visible just after the QRS (retrograde); abrupt onset/offset; responds to vagal manoeuvres and IV adenosine; definitive treatment: radiofrequency catheter ablation
options.C: Sinus tachycardia — normal physiological response to exercise
options.D: Ventricular tachycardia — broad complex, requires immediate DC cardioversion
options.E: Atrial flutter — sawtooth pattern at 300/min

explanation.correct: AV nodal re-entrant tachycardia (AVNRT): the most common paroxysmal SVT in adults (accounts for ~60% of SVTs). Mechanism: dual AV nodal pathways (fast and slow) create a re-entrant circuit; typically slow-fast AVNRT — conduction down the slow pathway and retrogradely up the fast pathway. ECG: regular narrow complex tachycardia 140-220/min; P waves buried within or just after the QRS (retrograde atrial activation near-simultaneous with ventricular). Symptoms: abrupt onset/offset palpitations (classically described as pounding in the neck), dizziness. Per NICE NG196: acute termination: vagal manoeuvres (Valsalva, carotid sinus massage) → IV adenosine (6mg rapid bolus IV; if no response 12mg; monitor for bronchospasm — withhold in asthmatics). Prevention: beta-blockers, flecainide (if no structural heart disease), verapamil. Definitive: radiofrequency catheter ablation (>95% cure rate).
explanation.A: Incorrect — AF is irregularly irregular with no P waves and a chaotic baseline. This tachycardia is regular.
explanation.B: CORRECT — AVNRT: regular narrow complex SVT at 150-220/min, P waves in/after QRS, abrupt onset/offset. Adenosine for acute termination; ablation for cure per NICE NG196.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Sinus tachycardia has clearly visible P waves before each QRS, gradual onset/offset, and rate rarely exceeds 150/min at rest.
explanation.D: Incorrect — VT is broad complex (QRS >0.12s). This is narrow complex — AVNRT.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Atrial flutter has characteristic sawtooth flutter waves at 300/min with ventricular rate typically 150/min (2:1 block).

reference: NICE NG196 — Atrial fibrillation and arrhythmias. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng196

question: A 35-year-old man presents to the GP with palpitations. During the episode his ECG shows: regular narrow complex tachycardia at 196/min with a short PR interval of 0.09 seconds and a delta wave visible on the initial upstroke of the QRS on the resting ECG. Per guidelines, what is the diagnosis and important management consideration?

options.A: Sinus tachycardia — no action needed
options.B: Wolff-Parkinson-White (WPW) syndrome — accessory pathway (Bundle of Kent) bypasses the AV node causing ventricular pre-excitation (short PR, delta wave on resting ECG); in AF, the accessory pathway can conduct very rapidly to the ventricles causing ventricular rates >300/min and ventricular fibrillation; AVOID AV-nodal blocking drugs (adenosine, beta-blockers, verapamil, digoxin) if AF develops with WPW — they may accelerate accessory pathway conduction; refer to electrophysiology for catheter ablation (curative)
options.C: Brugada syndrome — avoid sodium channel blockers and arrange ICD
options.D: Long QT syndrome — avoid QT-prolonging drugs
options.E: AVNRT — adenosine is safe and first-line in all narrow complex SVTs

explanation.correct: Wolff-Parkinson-White (WPW) syndrome: congenital accessory conduction pathway (Bundle of Kent) connecting atria to ventricles, bypassing the AV node. Resting ECG: short PR (<0.12s), delta wave (slurred upstroke of QRS due to ventricular pre-excitation), widened QRS. During SVT: usually orthodromic AVRT — narrow complex tachycardia (conduction down AV node, retrograde up accessory pathway). CRITICAL RISK: if AF develops in WPW, the accessory pathway can conduct extremely rapidly to the ventricles (>300/min) → ventricular fibrillation → sudden cardiac death. CONTRAINDICATED in WPW with AF: adenosine, beta-blockers, verapamil, diltiazem, digoxin — these block the AV node but may facilitate rapid conduction via the accessory pathway. Management of WPW with AF: IV flecainide or DC cardioversion. Definitive treatment: electrophysiology study + radiofrequency catheter ablation (>95% cure). Refer ALL WPW patients to electrophysiology.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Short PR + delta wave + SVT is WPW, not sinus tachycardia. This diagnosis carries a risk of sudden cardiac death if unrecognised.
explanation.B: CORRECT — WPW: short PR, delta wave, accessory pathway. Avoid AV-nodal blockers if AF develops (VF risk). Electrophysiology referral for ablation.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Brugada syndrome shows right bundle branch block pattern with ST elevation in V1-V3 — not delta waves and short PR.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Long QT syndrome shows prolonged QT interval — not short PR and delta wave.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Adenosine is specifically CONTRAINDICATED in WPW with AF. It can precipitate rapid accessory pathway conduction and VF. This is a critical prescribing safety point.

reference: ESC Guidelines — SVT management 2019. https://www.escardio.org/Guidelines

question: A 24-year-old woman with asthma is 22 weeks pregnant and has an acute asthma attack in the GP surgery. Her peak flow is 210 L/min (her personal best is 480 L/min = 44% of best). She is breathless at rest but can speak in sentences. Per BTS/SIGN asthma guidelines and RCOG guidance, what is the severity and acute management?

options.A: Mild attack — give salbutamol 2 puffs via spacer and review in 1 hour
options.B: Moderate to severe acute asthma — peak flow 44% of best indicates a moderate-severe attack; give salbutamol 2.5-5 mg nebuliser and ipratropium 0.5mg nebuliser; oral prednisolone 40-50 mg (or IV hydrocortisone 100 mg); oxygen to maintain SpO2 94-98%; call 999/arrange urgent hospital admission; fetal monitoring is important in severe asthma in pregnancy
options.C: Near-fatal attack — immediate intubation and ventilation in the GP surgery
options.D: Give salbutamol inhaler and monitor at home — prednisolone is contraindicated in pregnancy
options.E: Refer to obstetrics only — respiratory conditions in pregnancy are managed by obstetricians

explanation.correct: Per BTS/SIGN asthma guidelines: acute asthma severity classification: Moderate: PEFR 50-75% best/predicted, SpO2 ≥92%, can talk. Severe: PEFR 33-50% best, SpO2 ≥92%, difficulty talking. Life-threatening: PEFR <33% best, SpO2 <92%, exhaustion, silent chest, cyanosis. This patient: PEFR 44% = severe. Management: salbutamol 2.5-5 mg nebulised (repeat every 20 minutes); ipratropium 0.5 mg nebulised; oral prednisolone 40-50 mg (IV hydrocortisone 100 mg if unable to swallow); oxygen (target SpO2 94-98%); urgent hospital admission. Prednisolone IS safe in pregnancy (benefits outweigh risks) — per RCOG and BTS/SIGN: never withhold prednisolone from a pregnant woman with acute severe asthma. Fetal wellbeing monitoring needed. Magnesium sulphate IV 1.2-2g over 20 min if poor response.
explanation.A: Incorrect — PEFR 44% is not a mild attack — it is severe. Mild attack would be PEFR >75%.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Severe acute asthma: nebulised salbutamol + ipratropium + oral prednisolone + O2 + urgent hospital admission. Prednisolone IS safe in pregnancy per BTS/SIGN/RCOG.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Near-fatal asthma has PEFR <33% with SpO2 <92%, cyanosis, silent chest, exhaustion. This patient can speak in sentences.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Prednisolone is NOT contraindicated in pregnancy for acute severe asthma — withholding it risks maternal and fetal hypoxia.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Acute asthma in pregnancy is a medical emergency managed by the acute medical team with obstetric input, not by obstetrics alone.

reference: BTS/SIGN — Asthma guideline 2019. RCOG — Asthma in pregnancy. https://www.brit-thoracic.org.uk/quality-improvement/guidelines/asthma/

question: A 30-year-old pregnant woman at 28 weeks has her asthma reviewed. She is currently on salbutamol PRN only and has daily symptoms and 3 night wakings per week. Per NICE NG80 and BTS/SIGN, at which treatment step does she sit and what should be added?

options.A: Step 1 — increase salbutamol dose only
options.B: Step 2 — daily symptoms and nocturnal symptoms indicate uncontrolled asthma at Step 1; add an inhaled corticosteroid (ICS — e.g. beclometasone 200-800 mcg daily); ICS is safe throughout pregnancy and is the most important preventer medication; do NOT withhold ICS in pregnancy — uncontrolled asthma carries greater risks to the fetus than ICS
options.C: Step 4 — all pregnant women need high-dose ICS plus LABA
options.D: No medication change — accept suboptimal control during pregnancy
options.E: Step 3 — add LABA before trying ICS first

explanation.correct: Per NICE NG80 and BTS/SIGN asthma management guidelines: BTS/SIGN stepwise approach: Step 1: SABA (salbutamol) PRN only — mild intermittent symptoms. Step 2: Low-dose ICS (e.g. beclometasone 200-400 mcg BDP equivalent daily) — when: symptoms >2/week OR nocturnal symptoms OR SABA use >2 days/week OR any nocturnal symptoms. This patient: daily symptoms + 3 night wakings/week → Step 2 treatment is clearly indicated. ICS safety in pregnancy: well-established safety profile throughout all trimesters; do NOT withhold ICS. Uncontrolled asthma in pregnancy → fetal hypoxia, IUGR, preterm delivery — risks far exceed any theoretical ICS risk. Step 3 (if Step 2 insufficient): add LABA (salmeterol or formoterol) to ICS. Step 4+: specialist review, additional agents.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Simply increasing salbutamol dose does not address the underlying airway inflammation — ICS preventer therapy is required.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Daily symptoms + nocturnal symptoms = Step 2: add ICS. ICS is safe in pregnancy. Greater risk from uncontrolled asthma per NICE NG80/BTS.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Step 4 (high-dose ICS + LABA + other agents) is for uncontrolled asthma despite lower step treatment. This patient is on Step 1 requiring Step 2.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Accepting poor asthma control in pregnancy is dangerous — uncontrolled asthma reduces fetal oxygenation and increases risk of prematurity and IUGR.
explanation.E: Incorrect — LABA should never be used as monotherapy or before ICS. BTS Step 2 is ICS first; LABA added at Step 3 only.

reference: NICE NG80 — Asthma. BTS/SIGN asthma guideline. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng80

question: A mother brings her 12-year-old daughter for her NHS vaccinations. The daughter has received all routine vaccinations to date. Per the NHS childhood immunisation schedule, which vaccine is she due at age 12-13 (school year 8)?

options.A: MMR booster — third dose at age 12
options.B: HPV vaccine (Gardasil 9) — offered to all girls AND boys aged 12-13 in Year 8; protects against HPV types 6, 11, 16, 18, 31, 33, 45, 52, 58; prevents cervical cancer, other anogenital cancers, and genital warts; 2-dose schedule (0 and 6-12 months) if started before age 15; 3-dose schedule if started age 15 or older
options.C: Hepatitis B booster — routine booster at age 12
options.D: Varicella vaccine — offered to all 12-year-olds without prior chickenpox
options.E: BCG vaccine — routine booster at age 12

explanation.correct: Per NHS childhood immunisation schedule (current 2024): at age 12-13 (Year 8): HPV vaccine (Gardasil 9 — 9-valent HPV vaccine protecting against HPV 6, 11, 16, 18, 31, 33, 45, 52, 58). Since September 2019: offered to ALL children (girls AND boys) in Year 8. Why: protects against: HPV 16/18 — cause 70% of cervical cancers; HPV 31/33/45/52/58 — cause additional 20% of cervical cancers; HPV 6/11 — cause 90% of genital warts; other HPV-related cancers (oropharyngeal, anal, vulval, vaginal, penile). Dosing schedule: 2 doses (0 and 6-12 months apart) if first dose given before age 15; 3 doses (0, 1-2, 6 months) if started age 15+. Catch-up to age 25 for those who missed school programme. BCG is no longer routine but offered to high-risk neonates. No routine booster for hepatitis B, MMR (2 doses already given), or varicella (not on NHS routine schedule).
explanation.A: Incorrect — MMR is given at 1 year and 3 years 4 months (pre-school booster). There is no routine MMR booster at age 12.
explanation.B: CORRECT — HPV vaccine (Gardasil 9) is the Year 8 (age 12-13) vaccine for all children on the NHS schedule.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Hepatitis B is given in infancy (8, 12 and 16 weeks); there is no routine booster at age 12 on the NHS schedule.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Varicella vaccine is not on the routine NHS childhood immunisation schedule (offered to high-risk groups and healthcare workers but not universally).
explanation.E: Incorrect — BCG is no longer given routinely at age 13 on the NHS schedule; it is offered to high-risk neonates.

reference: NHS — Childhood immunisation schedule 2024. https://www.nhs.uk/vaccinations/nhs-vaccinations-and-when-to-have-them/

question: A practice nurse asks about the MMR vaccine schedule. A new GP registrar queries whether MMR is contraindicated in egg allergy. Per NICE CKS and PHE immunisation guidelines, what is the correct advice?

options.A: MMR is absolutely contraindicated in all children with any egg allergy
options.B: MMR vaccine is safe to administer in children with egg allergy including severe anaphylaxis to egg — the MMR vaccine is not grown on egg-containing medium; previous recommendations advising against MMR in egg allergy were based on outdated information; MMR should be given in the normal setting with standard 15-minute post-vaccination observation; specialist referral is only needed for anaphylaxis to a PREVIOUS DOSE of MMR itself
options.C: MMR can be given in mild egg allergy only; severe egg allergy requires hospital administration
options.D: A skin prick test with egg protein must be performed before MMR in any child with egg allergy
options.E: Only the measles component carries risk in egg allergy — give measles vaccine separately

explanation.correct: Per PHE/UKHSA 'The Green Book' (Immunisation against Infectious Disease) and NICE CKS: MMR vaccine IS SAFE in children with egg allergy including severe anaphylaxis to egg. Rationale: MMR (Priorix, M-M-RvaxPro) is produced in chick embryo fibroblast cell cultures — NOT in egg white. The residual ovalbumin content is extremely low (nanogram quantities) — insufficient to trigger anaphylaxis. Evidence: multiple large studies confirm MMR is safe in egg-allergic children including those with severe/anaphylactic reactions to egg. Current guidance: administer MMR in the normal community setting (GP surgery/school); observe for 15 minutes post-vaccination as standard; no need for hospital setting; no skin testing required. Exception: specialist referral is required for allergy to a PREVIOUS DOSE of MMR vaccine (not egg allergy) — possible reaction to neomycin or gelatin in the vaccine.
explanation.A: Incorrect — MMR is NOT contraindicated in egg allergy. This is outdated guidance that has been superseded by evidence and current PHE/NICE guidance.
explanation.B: CORRECT — MMR is safe in all egg allergy including severe anaphylaxis. No special precautions needed. Referral only for allergy to previous MMR dose per PHE Green Book.
explanation.C: Incorrect — There is no differentiation between mild and severe egg allergy for MMR administration — MMR is safe in all.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Skin prick testing before MMR is not required or recommended in egg allergy per PHE guidance.
explanation.E: Incorrect — The three components of MMR are formulated together and all are safe in egg allergy. Separate vaccines are not available or recommended.

reference: PHE — The Green Book: Immunisation against Infectious Disease. https://www.gov.uk/government/collections/immunisation-against-infectious-disease-the-green-book

question: A 45-year-old woman presents with a 4-week history of blood-stained nipple discharge from the right breast. She has no palpable lump. Her mammogram is normal. Per NICE NG12, what is the appropriate management?

options.A: Reassure — normal mammogram excludes malignancy
options.B: Urgent 2WW referral to breast clinic — blood-stained nipple discharge in a woman ≥50 should be referred on a suspected cancer pathway; in women under 50, non-blood-stained discharge alone from a single duct is the typical presentation of ductal papilloma; however blood-stained discharge at any age warrants urgent assessment; ductal papilloma is the most common benign cause but ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS) and malignancy must be excluded
options.C: Prescribe bromocriptine and repeat in 3 months
options.D: No further investigation — ductal papilloma always resolves spontaneously
options.E: Refer routinely (not urgently) to breast clinic within 18 weeks

explanation.correct: Blood-stained nipple discharge: always requires investigation to exclude malignancy. Causes: intraductal papilloma (most common benign cause — benign polyp within the lactiferous duct), ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS), invasive carcinoma, duct ectasia (usually brown/green discharge). Per NICE NG12 (Suspected cancer): blood-stained nipple discharge in women ≥50 = urgent suspected cancer referral (2WW). In women under 50: urgent referral is still recommended for blood-stained discharge. A normal mammogram does NOT exclude ductal pathology — mammography is relatively insensitive for intraductal lesions. Assessment in breast clinic: clinical examination, breast USS, ductography/galactography, ductoscopy, or surgical microdochectomy (excision of the affected duct — both diagnostic and therapeutic for ductal papilloma). Ductal papilloma: benign; presents with intermittent blood-stained/serous unilateral single-duct discharge; treated by surgical excision.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Normal mammogram does not exclude intraductal pathology or DCIS; blood-stained nipple discharge requires breast clinic assessment regardless.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Blood-stained nipple discharge: urgent breast clinic referral to exclude DCIS and malignancy per NICE NG12. Ductal papilloma is the common benign cause.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Bromocriptine suppresses prolactin and is used for galactorrhoea — not for blood-stained nipple discharge.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Ductal papilloma does not always resolve spontaneously and blood-stained discharge requires exclusion of malignancy; surgical excision is often required.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Routine 18-week referral is not appropriate for blood-stained nipple discharge — urgent/suspected cancer pathway referral is required per NICE NG12.

reference: NICE NG12 — Suspected cancer: recognition and referral. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng12

question: A 38-year-old woman presents with clear watery discharge from both nipples when expressed. She is not pregnant or breastfeeding. Her prolactin is 3,200 mIU/L (elevated). She takes no medications. Per NICE CKS, what is the most important diagnosis to exclude and what is the investigation?

options.A: This is physiological — reassure without investigation
options.B: Prolactinoma — a prolactin-secreting pituitary adenoma is the most common pituitary tumour; elevated prolactin in a non-pregnant, non-breastfeeding woman with galactorrhoea requires MRI pituitary with gadolinium; treatment: dopamine agonist (cabergoline preferred over bromocriptine for tolerability) reduces prolactin and tumour size
options.C: Hypothyroidism — check TSH only; TSH stimulates prolactin
options.D: Breast cancer — urgent 2WW mammogram
options.E: Ductal papilloma — refer for microdochectomy

explanation.correct: Hyperprolactinaemia with galactorrhoea: causes — physiological (pregnancy, breastfeeding), drug-induced (dopamine antagonists: antipsychotics, metoclopramide, domperidone, methyldopa), hypothyroidism (TRH stimulates prolactin), prolactinoma, renal failure (reduced clearance), macroprolactinaemia. This patient: no pregnancy, no breastfeeding, no medications → prolactinoma is the most important diagnosis to exclude. Per NICE CKS: MRI pituitary with gadolinium is the investigation of choice for suspected prolactinoma. Also check: TSH (hypothyroidism raises prolactin), renal function, drug history. Prolactinomas: microadenoma (<10 mm) or macroadenoma (≥10 mm — may cause visual field defects from optic chiasm compression). Treatment: cabergoline (dopamine agonist — D2 receptor agonist, suppresses prolactin secretion; very effective at reducing tumour size); bromocriptine (alternative — more side effects). Surgery: reserved for cabergoline-resistant or visual field compromise cases.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Galactorrhoea with elevated prolactin in a non-pregnant, non-breastfeeding woman is not physiological — prolactinoma must be excluded urgently.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Prolactinoma: most likely cause of elevated prolactin + galactorrhoea in non-pregnant woman with no medications. MRI pituitary + cabergoline treatment per NICE CKS.
explanation.C: Incorrect — TSH should be checked but is not the priority investigation; MRI pituitary is more urgent given significantly elevated prolactin without other obvious cause.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Clear bilateral expressed discharge with elevated prolactin is galactorrhoea from hyperprolactinaemia — not blood-stained discharge from malignancy.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Ductal papilloma causes blood-stained or serous unilateral single-duct discharge — not bilateral milky galactorrhoea with elevated prolactin.

reference: NICE CKS — Hyperprolactinaemia. https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/hyperprolactinaemia/

question: A 52-year-old man presents with proximal muscle weakness, hypokalaemia (K+ 2.9 mmol/L) and hypertension. His serum cortisol is very high (>3000 nmol/L) and ACTH is elevated at 95 pg/ml. He has no features of classic Cushing's syndrome (no striae, no moon face). Per NICE CKS, what type of Cushing's and what is the most likely cause?

options.A: ACTH-independent Cushing's — adrenal adenoma causing excess cortisol with suppressed ACTH
options.B: Ectopic ACTH syndrome — extremely high cortisol + elevated ACTH + severe hypokalaemia + rapid onset without classic cushingoid features; most commonly from small cell lung cancer, bronchial carcinoid, or thymoma; investigate with CT chest/abdomen/pelvis + high-dose dexamethasone suppression test (ectopic ACTH fails to suppress); refer urgently to endocrinology
options.C: Cushing's disease — pituitary adenoma; classic features always present
options.D: Exogenous steroid use — most common cause of Cushing's overall
options.E: Adrenal carcinoma — surgical resection is first-line

explanation.correct: Ectopic ACTH syndrome: non-pituitary, non-adrenal tumour secreting ACTH independently. Key distinguishing features from Cushing's disease (pituitary): extremely high cortisol (often >2000-3000 nmol/L — much higher than pituitary-driven Cushing's); severe hypokalaemia (ACTH-driven mineralocorticoid excess — aldosterone-independent); rapid onset; often NO classic Cushingoid features (rapid tumour progression means insufficient time to develop typical appearance); weight loss (from the primary tumour). ACTH is elevated (rules out adrenal cause — which suppresses ACTH). Common causes: small cell lung carcinoma (most common malignant cause), bronchial carcinoid, thymic carcinoid, medullary thyroid carcinoma, islet cell tumours. Per NICE CKS: High-dose dexamethasone suppression test — cortisol suppresses in Cushing's disease (pituitary) but NOT in ectopic ACTH or adrenal disease. CT chest/abdomen/pelvis; Gallium DOTATATE PET for carcinoid. Treatment: treat the primary tumour; metyrapone or ketoconazole to control cortisol pending definitive treatment.
explanation.A: Incorrect — ACTH-independent Cushing's (adrenal adenoma) would show LOW/suppressed ACTH (negative feedback from autonomous cortisol). This patient has elevated ACTH.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Ectopic ACTH: very high cortisol + elevated ACTH + severe hypokalaemia + no classic Cushingoid features. CT chest + high-dose dexamethasone test per NICE CKS.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Cushing's disease (pituitary) also has elevated ACTH but typically causes classic Cushingoid features and moderately elevated cortisol; it PARTIALLY suppresses on high-dose dexamethasone. Ectopic ACTH does not suppress.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Exogenous steroids are the most common OVERALL cause but would suppress endogenous ACTH and cortisol — not cause very high ACTH.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Adrenal carcinoma causes ACTH-independent Cushing's with suppressed (low) ACTH, not elevated ACTH.

reference: NICE CKS — Cushing's syndrome. https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/cushings-syndrome/

question: A 44-year-old woman with confirmed Cushing's disease (pituitary microadenoma on MRI) has morning cortisol of 890 nmol/L and has failed high-dose dexamethasone suppression. Per NICE CKS and endocrinology guidelines, what is the first-line treatment?

options.A: Long-term metyrapone — this is the definitive treatment for Cushing's disease
options.B: Transsphenoidal surgical resection of the pituitary adenoma — first-line treatment for Cushing's disease; remission rates 65-90% in expert centres; if surgery fails or is contraindicated: radiotherapy (pituitary-directed stereotactic radiosurgery) and/or cortisol-lowering drugs (metyrapone, ketoconazole, cabergoline, pasireotide); bilateral adrenalectomy as last resort (causes Nelson's syndrome — ACTH-secreting pituitary tumour enlargement)
options.C: Adrenalectomy — remove both adrenal glands as the primary approach
options.D: Oral prednisolone — reduces ACTH feedback
options.E: Spironolactone — manages the mineralocorticoid effects

explanation.correct: Cushing's disease: pituitary-driven Cushing's syndrome from an ACTH-secreting pituitary adenoma. Per NICE CKS and Endocrine Society guidelines: first-line treatment is transsphenoidal surgical resection — neurosurgeon removes the adenoma via the nasal passage and sphenoid sinus; minimally invasive; remission (cortisol normalisation) in 65-90% in experienced pituitary centres. Remission definition: post-operative cortisol <50 nmol/L. If surgical failure or recurrence: repeat surgery, pituitary radiotherapy (Gamma Knife stereotactic radiosurgery), medical therapy (metyrapone — 11-beta-hydroxylase inhibitor; ketoconazole — steroid synthesis inhibitor; cabergoline — reduces ACTH from some adenomas; pasireotide — somatostatin analogue reducing ACTH), or bilateral adrenalectomy. Nelson's syndrome: after bilateral adrenalectomy, removal of negative feedback causes rapid ACTH-secreting pituitary tumour enlargement — hyperpigmentation + mass effects.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Metyrapone reduces cortisol synthesis and can be used as bridge therapy or second-line, but it is NOT the definitive first-line treatment — surgery is.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Transsphenoidal surgery is first-line for Cushing's disease (pituitary adenoma) per NICE CKS/Endocrine Society.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Bilateral adrenalectomy is a last resort option (causes Nelson's syndrome) — not first-line.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Oral prednisolone would worsen Cushing's syndrome further — it has no role in treating it.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Spironolactone may manage some mineralocorticoid effects symptomatically but does not treat the underlying cause.

reference: NICE CKS — Cushing's syndrome. https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/cushings-syndrome/

question: A forest plot from a systematic review on statin therapy shows 8 randomised controlled trials. The overall pooled effect estimate (diamond) shows a relative risk of 0.78 (95% CI 0.65-0.91). The I² statistic is 72%. Per EBM principles, how should this result be interpreted?

options.A: The result is definitive — RR 0.78 is highly statistically significant so clinical heterogeneity is irrelevant
options.B: The pooled RR of 0.78 (95% CI 0.65-0.91) suggests statins reduce the relative risk by 22% (CI does not cross 1.0 = statistically significant); however I² = 72% indicates HIGH heterogeneity between studies (I² >50% is considered high); this means the studies are not all measuring the same thing — differences in populations, doses, follow-up, or outcomes may explain the variability; a pooled estimate should be interpreted with caution when I² is high; investigate sources of heterogeneity
options.C: I² of 72% means 72% of studies showed benefit — this is a positive finding
options.D: The 95% CI of 0.65-0.91 means the drug is harmful in 9% of patients
options.E: A result is only significant if the 95% CI is entirely below 0.5

explanation.correct: Forest plot and meta-analysis interpretation: RR 0.78 (95% CI 0.65-0.91): statins reduce the risk of the outcome by 22% relative to control; CI does not include 1.0 = statistically significant (p<0.05). I² statistic: measures the proportion of total variation between studies due to heterogeneity (rather than sampling error/chance). Interpretation: I² 0-25%: low heterogeneity; 25-50%: moderate; 50-75%: high; >75%: very high. I² = 72% = HIGH heterogeneity — the studies differ substantially in their results. This does not invalidate the meta-analysis but means: the pooled estimate should be treated cautiously; sources of heterogeneity (populations, doses, outcomes, follow-up duration) should be explored via subgroup analysis; the meta-analysis should ideally use a random-effects model (not fixed-effects) when I² is high.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Statistical significance (CI not crossing 1.0) and clinical heterogeneity (I²) are independent concerns; high I² raises important questions about whether pooling was appropriate.
explanation.B: CORRECT — RR 0.78 is significant (CI 0.65-0.91 does not cross 1.0); but I² 72% = high heterogeneity; interpret pooled estimate cautiously and investigate heterogeneity sources.
explanation.C: Incorrect — I² measures percentage of variability due to heterogeneity between studies — not the proportion of studies showing benefit.
explanation.D: Incorrect — The 95% CI means if the study were repeated 100 times, 95% of the CIs would contain the true RR. It does not mean the drug harms a proportion of patients.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Statistical significance requires the 95% CI to not cross the null value (RR=1.0 for relative risk; RR <1.0 = benefit). The threshold is 1.0, not 0.5.

reference: BMJ Statistics Notes — Forest plots and meta-analysis. Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews.

question: A GP reads a study showing that a new diabetes drug reduces HbA1c by 8 mmol/mol (SD 4) compared to placebo. The p-value is p=0.04 and the 95% CI is 0.2-15.8 mmol/mol. The study included 45 patients. Per EBM principles, what is the correct interpretation?

options.A: The result is clinically and statistically significant — this drug should immediately be adopted
options.B: The result is statistically significant (p=0.04; CI does not cross zero) but the wide 95% CI (0.2-15.8) reflects a small sample size and large uncertainty; the minimum clinically important difference (MCID) for HbA1c reduction is approximately 5-6 mmol/mol; the lower confidence bound (0.2) may be below the MCID — meaning a real-world effect could be minimal; the result is preliminary and needs replication in a larger, adequately powered trial before practice change
options.C: p=0.04 is borderline and means there is a 4% chance the treatment works
options.D: The standard deviation of 4 means the result is not significant
options.E: A 95% CI of 0.2-15.8 means the drug works in 95% of patients

explanation.correct: Statistical versus clinical significance: this study is statistically significant (p=0.04; 95% CI does not include zero — positive values only). However: (1) Small sample (n=45) — underpowered studies produce wide CIs; (2) Wide CI (0.2-15.8): the true effect could be anywhere from barely detectable (0.2 mmol/mol) to very large (15.8 mmol/mol); (3) MCID for HbA1c: approximately 5-6 mmol/mol is considered the minimum clinically meaningful change — the lower CI limit of 0.2 is well below this, meaning a real-world effect of marginal benefit is possible; (4) Interpretation of p-value: p=0.04 means 'if the null hypothesis (no difference) were true, there is a 4% probability of obtaining a result this extreme or more extreme by chance' — it does NOT mean there is a 4% chance the drug works or a 96% chance it works. Practice change should await adequately powered trials with consistent results.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Statistical significance alone (especially in a small study with wide CI) is insufficient to justify immediate adoption into practice.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Statistically significant but wide CI from small sample; lower bound may be below MCID; needs larger replication trial before practice change.
explanation.C: Incorrect — p=0.04 means 4% probability of the observed result under the null hypothesis — NOT that the drug has a 4% probability of working.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Standard deviation describes within-group variability around the mean — it does not by itself determine statistical significance.
explanation.E: Incorrect — 95% CI means 95% probability that the interval contains the true population mean difference — NOT that the drug works in 95% of patients.

reference: BMJ Statistics Notes — Confidence intervals. https://www.bmj.com/about-bmj/resources-readers/publications/statistics-square-one

question: A GP is calculating statistics from a screening test for coeliac disease. In a population of 1,000: 100 truly have coeliac disease, 900 do not. The test correctly identifies 90 of the 100 with coeliac disease. The test incorrectly identifies 45 of the 900 without coeliac disease as positive. Per EBM, calculate the positive predictive value (PPV) and negative predictive value (NPV).

options.A: PPV = 90%, NPV = 95% — sensitivity and PPV are the same statistic
options.B: PPV = 67% (90 true positives ÷ 135 total positives × 100); NPV = 98.8% (855 true negatives ÷ 865 total negatives × 100) — PPV and NPV depend on disease prevalence in the tested population, unlike sensitivity and specificity
options.C: PPV = 90%, NPV = 90% — both equal sensitivity
options.D: PPV cannot be calculated without knowing the specificity
options.E: PPV = 45%, NPV = 45% — based on the false positive rate

explanation.correct: From the data: TP=90 (true positives), FN=10 (missed cases), FP=45 (false positives), TN=855 (true negatives). Totals: Test positive = TP+FP = 90+45 = 135; Test negative = TN+FN = 855+10 = 865. PPV = TP/(TP+FP) = 90/135 = 66.7% ≈ 67%. This means: of all positive tests, 67% are true positives (33% are false positives). NPV = TN/(TN+FN) = 855/865 = 98.8%. This means: of all negative tests, 98.8% are true negatives (1.2% are false negatives — missed cases). Sensitivity = TP/(TP+FN) = 90/100 = 90% (ability to detect true cases). Specificity = TN/(TN+FP) = 855/900 = 95% (ability to correctly exclude non-cases). KEY POINT: PPV and NPV depend on disease prevalence — the same test will have lower PPV in a low-prevalence population and higher PPV in a high-prevalence population. Sensitivity and specificity are inherent test characteristics that do not change with prevalence.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Sensitivity (90%) and PPV (67%) are different statistics. Sensitivity measures the test's ability to detect disease; PPV measures the probability that a positive test result is truly positive.
explanation.B: CORRECT — PPV = 90/135 = 67%; NPV = 855/865 = 98.8%. PPV and NPV are prevalence-dependent.
explanation.C: Incorrect — PPV and NPV are calculated from different 2×2 table denominators and will not equal each other or sensitivity unless under very specific mathematical conditions.
explanation.D: Incorrect — PPV can be calculated directly from the 2×2 table data given without needing to calculate specificity separately.
explanation.E: Incorrect — False positive rate (1-specificity) = 45/900 = 5% — not used to calculate PPV or NPV.

reference: BMJ Statistics Notes — Sensitivity, specificity, PPV, NPV. https://www.bmj.com/about-bmj/resources-readers/publications/statistics-square-one

question: A GP reads a cohort study: among 500 smokers, 50 developed lung cancer over 10 years. Among 1,000 non-smokers, 10 developed lung cancer. Per EBM, calculate the relative risk (RR) and absolute risk increase (ARI) for smokers versus non-smokers.

options.A: RR = 5, ARI = 5% — smoking increases relative risk fivefold and absolute risk by 5%
options.B: RR = 10, ARI = 9% — smokers have 10x the relative risk; the absolute risk increases from 1% (non-smokers) to 10% (smokers), an absolute difference of 9%; NNH = 100/9 = 11 (11 smokers would need to smoke for one additional case of lung cancer compared to non-smokers)
options.C: RR = 2, ARI = 2% — relative risk is doubled
options.D: RR = 0.5, ARI = -5% — non-smokers have lower risk so RR <1
options.E: ARI and RR cannot be calculated from cohort data — only from RCTs

explanation.correct: Calculations: Risk in smokers (exposed) = 50/500 = 0.10 = 10%. Risk in non-smokers (unexposed) = 10/1000 = 0.01 = 1%. Relative Risk (RR) = Risk(exposed) ÷ Risk(unexposed) = 10% ÷ 1% = 10. Interpretation: Smokers have 10 times the risk of lung cancer compared to non-smokers. Absolute Risk Increase (ARI) = Risk(exposed) - Risk(unexposed) = 10% - 1% = 9%. Interpretation: smoking causes 9 additional cases per 100 smokers over 10 years compared to non-smokers. Number Needed to Harm (NNH) = 1/ARI = 1/0.09 = 11. Key teaching point: RR gives the relative scale of risk (impressive-sounding: 10x) while ARI gives the absolute scale (practical: 9% absolute difference); both are essential to present for informed patient decision-making. RR alone without ARI can mislead — a RR of 10 is very different from a baseline risk of 0.0001% vs 0.001% compared to 1% vs 10%.
explanation.A: Incorrect — RR = 10% ÷ 1% = 10, not 5. ARI = 10% - 1% = 9%, not 5%.
explanation.B: CORRECT — RR = 10 (10-fold increase); ARI = 9% (9 additional cases per 100); NNH = 11 per EBM calculation.
explanation.C: Incorrect — RR = 2 would mean risk doubles (e.g. 2% vs 1%). Here risk is 10x higher (10% vs 1%).
explanation.D: Incorrect — RR is calculated as exposed ÷ unexposed. Smokers have higher risk → RR >1.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Relative risk and absolute risk increase can be calculated from cohort studies (and RCTs). Odds ratios are used in case-control studies.

reference: BMJ Statistics Notes — Risk ratios and absolute risk. https://www.bmj.com/about-bmj/resources-readers/publications/statistics-square-one

question: A 28-year-old woman is investigated for iron deficiency anaemia with no obvious cause. Anti-tissue transglutaminase IgA antibodies (anti-tTG IgA) are strongly positive (×10 upper limit of normal). Her total IgA is normal. Per NICE NG20, what is the next step to confirm the diagnosis?

options.A: Start a gluten-free diet immediately — anti-tTG positivity confirms coeliac disease
options.B: Refer for gastroscopy with duodenal biopsy — duodenal biopsy (minimum 4 samples including 1 from the duodenal bulb) is the gold standard for confirming coeliac disease; biopsy shows villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia and intraepithelial lymphocytosis (Marsh classification); the patient must continue a GLUTEN-CONTAINING diet until after biopsy
options.C: Repeat anti-tTG in 3 months — one positive result is insufficient
options.D: HLA-DQ2/DQ8 genetic testing is needed before biopsy
options.E: Capsule endoscopy is the investigation of choice for coeliac disease confirmation

explanation.correct: Per NICE NG20 (Coeliac disease): serology (anti-tTG IgA or anti-endomysial antibodies IgA) is the first-line screening test. A strongly positive anti-tTG (>10× ULN) has a high positive predictive value for coeliac disease but a BIOPSY is still required to confirm the diagnosis in adults (exceptions: adults with strongly positive anti-tTG >10×ULN may be eligible for a non-biopsy diagnosis pathway in some centres if supported by positive HLA-DQ2/DQ8 and symptoms — per updated BSG guidelines). Gastroscopy with duodenal biopsy: minimum 4 biopsies (2 from D1-D2, 1 from duodenal bulb) while on a GLUTEN-CONTAINING diet — if patient has already started GFD, the biopsy will be falsely normal; Marsh grading: Marsh 1 (lymphocytosis only), Marsh 2 (crypt hyperplasia), Marsh 3 (villous atrophy — graded A/B/C). Diagnosis confirmed: histology + serology + clinical response to GFD.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Starting a GFD before biopsy will cause villous healing and false-negative biopsy. Never start GFD until biopsy is complete per NICE NG20.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Gastroscopy + duodenal biopsy on gluten-containing diet is the gold standard to confirm coeliac disease per NICE NG20.
explanation.C: Incorrect — A strongly positive anti-tTG (×10 ULN) is a clear positive result; repeating serology delays diagnosis. Biopsy is the next step.
explanation.D: Incorrect — HLA-DQ2/DQ8 testing is used to exclude coeliac disease in ambiguous cases (>99% of coeliac patients are HLA-DQ2 or DQ8 positive); it is not routinely required before biopsy.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Capsule endoscopy is used for refractory coeliac disease or suspected complications — not routine first-line confirmation.

reference: NICE NG20 — Coeliac disease. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng20

question: A 34-year-old woman with confirmed coeliac disease has been on a strict gluten-free diet for 18 months. Her anti-tTG antibodies have normalised. She asks her GP when she should have a repeat duodenal biopsy to confirm mucosal healing. Per NICE NG20 and BSG guidelines, what is the recommendation?

options.A: No follow-up biopsy is ever needed once anti-tTG normalises
options.B: A follow-up duodenal biopsy after 12-24 months of strict gluten-free diet is recommended to confirm mucosal healing (villous architecture restored); persistent villous atrophy despite dietary compliance may indicate refractory coeliac disease or inadvertent gluten exposure; anti-tTG normalisation alone does not reliably confirm complete mucosal healing in all patients
options.C: Biopsy should be repeated every 5 years indefinitely
options.D: Biopsy should be performed immediately after starting the GFD (at 3 months)
options.E: Follow-up biopsy is only needed if anti-tTG remains positive at 12 months

explanation.correct: Per NICE NG20 and BSG coeliac guidelines: a follow-up duodenal biopsy after 12-24 months of strict gluten-free diet is recommended in most adults to confirm mucosal healing. Why: anti-tTG antibody normalisation is a good marker of dietary compliance and improving disease but does not perfectly correlate with mucosal healing — studies show up to 30-40% of adults with normalised serology still have persistent villous atrophy on biopsy. Identifying persistent atrophy is important: it may indicate refractory coeliac disease (rare but associated with enteropathy-associated T-cell lymphoma risk), ongoing inadvertent gluten exposure, or alternative diagnoses (microscopic colitis, CVID). Response biopsy: same minimum 4 samples from duodenum. However: BSG 2023 update acknowledges that in patients who are asymptomatic with strongly normalised serology, the follow-up biopsy pathway is evolving and not universally mandatory — discuss with individual patients and gastroenterology.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Anti-tTG normalisation does not guarantee complete mucosal healing; follow-up biopsy is recommended per NICE NG20.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Follow-up biopsy at 12-24 months of GFD confirms mucosal healing; normalised anti-tTG does not reliably confirm complete villous healing per NICE NG20/BSG.
explanation.C: Incorrect — 5-yearly biopsy is not the recommended routine follow-up schedule; biopsy at 12-24 months to confirm healing is the key checkpoint.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Mucosal healing takes 12-24 months on a strict GFD; a biopsy at 3 months would show incomplete healing and be unhelpful.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Follow-up biopsy is recommended even when anti-tTG has normalised, as mucosal healing cannot be assumed from serology alone.

reference: NICE NG20 — Coeliac disease. BSG coeliac guidelines. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng20

question: A GP is shown a box and whisker plot of blood pressure measurements from a clinical trial. The box contains a horizontal line in the middle. The box extends from the 25th to 75th percentile. Per EBM and statistical principles, what does the horizontal line in the middle of the box represent?

options.A: The mean blood pressure
options.B: The median (50th percentile) — the middle horizontal line in a box and whisker plot always represents the median; the box spans the interquartile range (IQR = 25th to 75th percentile); the whiskers extend to the minimum and maximum values (excluding outliers which are shown as individual dots beyond the whiskers)
options.C: The mode — the most frequently occurring value
options.D: The 95th percentile — the upper confidence interval
options.E: The standard deviation of the distribution

explanation.correct: Box and whisker plot anatomy: the horizontal line inside the box = the MEDIAN (50th percentile) — this is the middle value when all observations are ranked from lowest to highest. The box boundaries: lower edge = 25th percentile (Q1); upper edge = 75th percentile (Q3). Box height = IQR (interquartile range = Q3-Q1) — measures the spread of the middle 50% of data. Whiskers: extend to the lowest and highest values within 1.5×IQR from the box edges; data points beyond whiskers = outliers (plotted individually). Mean vs Median in box plots: box plots show the MEDIAN, not the mean; in skewed distributions the mean and median differ; box plots are preferred over histograms for showing distribution skewness and comparing multiple groups. AKT application: the examiner will show a box plot and ask you to identify the median, IQR, or identify an outlier — always remember the middle line = median, NOT mean.
explanation.A: Incorrect — The mean is not shown directly on a standard box and whisker plot. The middle horizontal line is the MEDIAN.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Middle line = median (50th percentile). Box = IQR (25th-75th percentile). Whiskers = range excluding outliers.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Mode (most common value) is not represented on a standard box and whisker plot.
explanation.D: Incorrect — The 95th percentile is not shown by the middle line of the box. The whisker endpoint may approximate the 5th-95th percentile range but is technically based on 1.5×IQR rule.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Standard deviation is not depicted in a box and whisker plot; it is used in normally distributed data. Box plots are preferred for non-normally distributed data.

reference: BMJ Statistics Notes — Box and whisker plots. https://www.bmj.com/about-bmj/resources-readers/publications/statistics-square-one

question: A clinical trial reports: mean SBP reduction with drug A = 12 mmHg (SD 8, n=100); mean SBP reduction with drug B = 9 mmHg (SD 7, n=100). The difference is 3 mmHg. Per EBM statistical principles, which statistical test is most appropriate to compare these two means?

options.A: Chi-squared test — compares proportions in two groups
options.B: Independent samples t-test — comparing two means from independent groups with continuous, approximately normally distributed data; appropriate here as: two independent groups (drug A vs drug B), continuous outcome (SBP in mmHg), sample size ≥30 (n=100 each — central limit theorem applies), similar standard deviations; result gives a t-statistic and p-value indicating whether the 3 mmHg difference is statistically significant
options.C: Mann-Whitney U test — always preferred over t-test for any clinical data
options.D: Paired t-test — used when the same patients are measured twice
options.E: ANOVA — required whenever comparing more than two data points

explanation.correct: Statistical test selection: (1) Type of outcome variable: continuous (SBP in mmHg) → parametric tests if normally distributed. (2) Number of groups: two groups (A vs B). (3) Independence: separate patients in each group → unpaired/independent test. (4) Distribution: n=100 → central limit theorem ensures approximate normality → parametric test appropriate. Independent samples t-test (Student's t-test): compares two independent group means; appropriate for continuous, approximately normally distributed data with independent groups. Produces: t-statistic, degrees of freedom, p-value, 95% CI for the mean difference. Alternative if non-normally distributed or small samples: Mann-Whitney U test (non-parametric equivalent). Chi-squared: for comparing proportions/categorical data (e.g. % of patients reaching target BP <130/80). Paired t-test: same patients measured before and after. ANOVA: 3 or more independent groups.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Chi-squared compares proportions/categorical outcomes (e.g. % patients reaching a threshold). SBP reduction is continuous — chi-squared is not appropriate.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Independent samples t-test: two independent groups, continuous outcome, large samples (n=100 — normal distribution assumed). Appropriate test for comparing two means.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Mann-Whitney U (non-parametric) is used when data is not normally distributed or samples are small. With n=100, the independent t-test is appropriate and more powerful.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Paired t-test is for paired/dependent data (e.g. same patient measured before and after treatment). These are two different patient groups — unpaired.
explanation.E: Incorrect — ANOVA is used when comparing means across 3 or more groups. Only two groups here.

reference: BMJ Statistics Notes — Statistical tests for comparing means. https://www.bmj.com/about-bmj/resources-readers/publications/statistics-square-one

question: A GP is reviewing a newly prescribed drug for a patient. The Patient Information Leaflet (PIL) shows a black inverted triangle symbol (▼) next to the drug name. Per MHRA guidance, what does this symbol indicate?

options.A: The drug is a controlled drug — special prescription requirements apply
options.B: The black triangle (▼) indicates that the medicine is subject to ADDITIONAL MONITORING by the MHRA; this usually applies to new medicines or those approved under exceptional circumstances where the evidence base is still being established; healthcare professionals and patients are strongly encouraged to report ALL suspected adverse reactions via the Yellow Card scheme (not just serious ones as for established drugs); the symbol appears in PILs and SPCs
options.C: The drug should not be used in patients under 18 — paediatric contraindication
options.D: The drug requires specialist initiation only — GPs cannot prescribe it
options.E: The drug has been withdrawn from the market but stocks are still being used

explanation.correct: Per MHRA (Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency): the black inverted triangle symbol (▼) on a medicine's PIL/SMP indicates it is subject to additional monitoring. Applies to: newly authorised medicines (less post-market safety data); medicines approved under exceptional circumstances; biosimilar medicines (to detect any differences from the reference biologic). Purpose: to facilitate rapid identification of new safety signals. Reporting: healthcare professionals and patients should report ALL suspected adverse reactions (not just serious ones) via the MHRA Yellow Card scheme (yellowcard.mhra.gov.uk or via the Yellow Card app). The symbol is used across the EU/UK since 2013. Medicines retain the ▼ symbol until sufficient post-market safety data has accumulated (typically 5 years). This is distinct from: CD (controlled drug) scheduling, which has different legal requirements; specialist-only prescribing restrictions (NICE/NHS England criteria).
explanation.A: Incorrect — Controlled drug status is indicated by 'CD' on the prescription and has specific legal requirements (schedule) — not the black triangle symbol.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Black triangle (▼) = additional monitoring; report ALL suspected ADRs via Yellow Card scheme per MHRA guidance.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Paediatric contraindications are stated in the prescribing information and PIL text, not indicated by the black triangle symbol.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Specialist-only prescribing is indicated in NHS England/NICE guidance or SLS endorsements — not the black triangle.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Withdrawn medicines are not in circulation; the black triangle applies to newly licensed medicines requiring additional surveillance.

reference: MHRA — Black triangle scheme. https://www.gov.uk/guidance/the-black-triangle-scheme

question: A GP identifies that a patient developed a serious adverse drug reaction (sudden onset hearing loss) from gentamicin prescribed in hospital. Per MHRA Yellow Card guidance, who can report this and what constitutes a reportable reaction?

options.A: Only hospital doctors can report reactions to drugs first prescribed in hospital
options.B: Any healthcare professional (GP, nurse, pharmacist) AND patients/carers can report suspected adverse drug reactions via the Yellow Card scheme; for established medicines: report serious, unexpected or unlisted reactions; for black triangle medicines: report ALL suspected reactions regardless of severity; for vaccines: report all suspected adverse reactions
options.C: Only serious reactions (ICU admission or death) qualify for Yellow Card reporting
options.D: The Yellow Card scheme is voluntary and rarely checked by the MHRA
options.E: Yellow Cards can only be submitted by the prescribing doctor

explanation.correct: Per MHRA Yellow Card scheme guidance: Who can report: any healthcare professional (doctor, dentist, nurse, pharmacist, coroner, etc.) AND patients, carers and members of the public. What to report: established medicines: suspected serious reactions (fatal, life-threatening, requiring hospitalisation, causing disability, congenital abnormality, or medically significant); any reaction considered unexpected or unlisted in the product information; black triangle medicines (▼): ALL suspected adverse reactions regardless of severity (even mild reactions); vaccines: ALL suspected adverse reactions; herbal and complementary products: ALL suspected reactions. Purpose: pharmacovigilance — detecting new safety signals, revising prescribing information, withdrawal of harmful medicines when necessary (e.g. withdrawal of vioxx, thalidomide history). Yellow Cards are taken seriously — they have directly contributed to regulatory action. GP's role: reporting from primary care is particularly valuable as it captures long-term and community adverse effects not seen in clinical trials.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Any healthcare professional or patient can report reactions via Yellow Card regardless of where the drug was originally prescribed.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Any HCP or patient can report; for established drugs: serious/unexpected reactions; for black triangle drugs: ALL reactions per MHRA Yellow Card guidance.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Serious reactions (ICU/death) are always reportable, but the threshold for reporting is broader and includes unexpected reactions and all reactions to black triangle drugs.
explanation.D: Incorrect — The Yellow Card scheme is actively monitored by the MHRA — it is a key pharmacovigilance tool that has led to regulatory action on multiple medicines.
explanation.E: Incorrect — The Yellow Card scheme is open to all healthcare professionals and patients, not restricted to the prescriber.

reference: MHRA — Yellow Card scheme. https://yellowcard.mhra.gov.uk/

question: A patient with confirmed cranial diabetes insipidus is prescribed desmopressin. The GP is deciding between oral desmopressin and intranasal desmopressin. During the water deprivation test, the endocrinologist administered desmopressin 2 mcg IM at t=8 hours. Per BNF and clinical pharmacology, what is the key difference in bioavailability between routes and why does it matter for dosing?

options.A: All routes are bioequivalent — dose is the same regardless of route
options.B: There is a large difference in bioavailability between routes: intranasal ~3-4% (higher than oral but lower than parenteral); oral tablets ~0.1-0.2%; parenteral/IM/IV ~100%; the oral dose is therefore much higher than the intranasal or parenteral dose for equivalent effect; for example: oral 120-240 mcg BD is roughly equivalent to intranasal 10-20 mcg BD; patients must never switch routes without dose adjustment as underdosing (DI recurrence) or overdosing (hyponatraemia) can result
options.C: Intranasal desmopressin has the same bioavailability as oral
options.D: Parenteral desmopressin cannot be used for DI — only for haemophilia
options.E: Dose adjustment between routes is not clinically significant for desmopressin

explanation.correct: Desmopressin bioavailability by route (per BNF and pharmacology): IV/IM (parenteral): ~100% bioavailability — used for acute testing (water deprivation test) and haemophilia/vWD (2-4 mcg IV/IM). Intranasal spray/drops: approximately 3-4% bioavailability — used for DI maintenance; dose: 10-40 mcg/day in 1-2 doses. Oral tablets: approximately 0.1-0.2% bioavailability — used for DI, nocturia, primary nocturnal enuresis; dose: 100-400 mcg 2-3 times daily. Sublingual (melt): slightly higher than oral tablets (~0.2-0.3%). The markedly lower oral bioavailability means the oral dose must be 50-100× higher than the intranasal dose for equivalent effect. Clinical significance: switching between routes without dose adjustment is DANGEROUS — can cause: under-treatment (recurrence of DI, hypernatraemia) or over-treatment (dilutional hyponatraemia from over-replacement). Always consult BNF/endocrinologist when switching routes.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Routes are NOT bioequivalent; there are large differences requiring substantial dose adjustments.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Oral bioavailability ~0.1-0.2% vs intranasal ~3-4% vs parenteral ~100%. Route switching requires dose adjustment; failure risks DI recurrence or hyponatraemia per BNF.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Intranasal desmopressin has approximately 20-40× higher bioavailability than oral tablets.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Parenteral desmopressin IS used for acute DI testing (water deprivation test) and for haemophilia A/vWD; both are licensed indications.
explanation.E: Incorrect — The difference in bioavailability is clinically critical — failure to adjust doses between routes has caused serious patient harm (hyponatraemia, seizures).

reference: BNF — Desmopressin. https://bnf.nice.org.uk/drug/desmopressin.html

question: A 19-year-old student presents with secondary enuresis (bed-wetting) for the past 3 months having previously been dry for years. He has no daytime symptoms. He is drinking 4-5 litres of water per day. Per NICE CKS, what differential diagnoses should be considered and what initial investigations should be requested?

options.A: This is normal behaviour in a stressed student — reassure without investigation
options.B: Secondary enuresis in a previously dry adult is a red flag — differentials include: cranial diabetes insipidus (polyuria from ADH deficiency), nephrogenic DI, diabetes mellitus (osmotic diuresis), psychogenic polydipsia, UTI; initial investigations: urine dipstick (glucose, protein, blood), fasting glucose/HbA1c, U&E, serum osmolality, urine osmolality (morning sample), TFTs
options.C: UTI only — urine culture and oral trimethoprim
options.D: Bladder overactivity — refer for urodynamics
options.E: Anxiety disorder — CBT referral

explanation.correct: Secondary enuresis (onset after a period of dryness) in an adult is always a red flag for an underlying pathology — unlike primary enuresis (never been dry). The history of polydipsia (4-5 litres/day) suggests a polyuric disorder. Per NICE CKS: differential diagnoses for adult secondary enuresis + polydipsia: Diabetes mellitus: osmotic diuresis from hyperglycaemia — most common cause; Cranial DI: ADH deficiency causing inability to concentrate urine; Nephrogenic DI: renal resistance to ADH; Psychogenic polydipsia: primary polydipsia without organic cause (psychiatric patients); UTI/LUTS: less likely with daytime dryness. First-line investigations: urine dipstick (glycosuria suggests DM; haematuria/proteinuria); random glucose or HbA1c; U&E (hypokalaemia in Conn's, hypernatraemia in DI); serum and urine osmolality (paired samples for DI assessment); TFTs (hyperthyroidism can cause polyuria). If DM excluded and DI suspected: water deprivation test.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Secondary enuresis in an adult with polydipsia requires investigation for underlying pathology including diabetes mellitus and DI — this cannot be dismissed.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Secondary enuresis + polydipsia: red flag; investigate DM (most common), DI, electrolytes, urine/serum osmolality per NICE CKS.
explanation.C: Incorrect — UTI would cause dysuria and daytime frequency — this patient has secondary enuresis with polydipsia suggesting a systemic polyuric disorder.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Bladder overactivity causes frequency, urgency and nocturia with normal fluid intake — not 4-5 litres/day polydipsia.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Anxiety may cause increased fluid intake but the degree of polydipsia (4-5 litres/day) and secondary enuresis requires organic exclusion before attributing to anxiety.

reference: NICE CKS — Enuresis in adults. Diabetes insipidus. https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/diabetes-insipidus/

question: A GP trainee raises a concern that their educational supervisor (a consultant) appears to be consistently preventing them from attending their mandatory study days by scheduling clinics at the same time. Per GMC and BMA guidance on workplace bullying and educational supervision, what is the appropriate escalation pathway?

options.A: Accept it — consultants have full authority over trainee schedules
options.B: Raise the concern first informally with the educational supervisor; if unresolved, escalate to the Training Programme Director (TPD)/Head of School; if still unresolved, contact the Foundation Programme Director, responsible officer, or the GMC (if patient safety is affected); document all instances; the BMA is available for support and advice; this constitutes potential bullying and undermining — both GMC-prohibited behaviours
options.C: Report directly to the GMC without speaking to anyone at the practice first
options.D: Submit an FOI request about the consultant's rota decisions
